summary:
MARS-NAV is an interactive web platform designed as an exploration and survival guide for astronauts and mission planners on Mars. Its main purpose is to bring together scientific information about different regions of the planet, using open data from NASA and records from missions such as Curiosity and Perseverance. Through an interactive map, users can explore coordinates, temperature, radiation levels, atmospheric pressure, terrain characteristics, and potential natural resources, as well as view real photographs captured by rovers.
The project addresses the challenges of Martian exploration by making it easier to analyze and compare different areas, helping identify potential risks and recognize locations that may offer better conditions for an expedition. To achieve this, it combines web technologies such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet.js, and Supabase.
We believe MARS-NAV is important because it transforms scientific data into more accessible and understandable information, supporting decision-making, route planning, and preparation for the conditions that future explorers may encounter on Mars.
details:
What does it do and how does it work? The system operates through an end-to-end pipeline that connects data science, artificial intelligence, and real-time web visualization:

  1. Processing and Machine Learning (Python + Scikit-Learn): Using a structured dataset with real Mars parameters (dataset_marte_ml.csv), the modelo.py module applies 2nd-degree Polynomial Regression over coordinates and elevation to predict surface temperatures (°C), radiation levels (mSv/day), and automatically classify the operational risk level (Moderate or Critical).
  2. Routing Engine and EVA Protocols (rutas.py): Evaluates terrain-adjusted distances on Mars, applies penalties for environmental hazards, and generates customized tactical survival protocols (4-hour EVA exposure limits, alerts for slopes greater than 15°, wind protocols for dust storms, and suit thermal management).
  3. Dynamic Generation and Integration (generar_json.py and generar_mapa.py): Packages the model's predictions into JSON format and injects them into the web interface synchronized with our cloud database (Supabase).
  4. HUD Cartographic Viewer (HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and Leaflet.js): Displays an interactive topographic map of the Aeolis-Elysium sector (MC-23). Clicking on any pulsing solar beacon triggers a camera fly-to animation toward the target and displays predictive telemetry, optimal routing strategies, and real photographs captured by NASA rovers.

Benefits and expected impact:

  • Safety in Extravehicular Activities (EVA): Anticipates critical zones with high radiation, steep slopes, or shifting sand dunes before deploying crew members or rovers.
  • Resource and route optimization: Calculates risk-weighted paths and facilitates the location of natural shelters (lava tubes) and mineral or water deposits (hydrated clays and subsurface ice).
  • Scientific scalability: Thanks to its predictive model in Python, the system can estimate environmental conditions at new Martian coordinates where permanent weather stations do not yet exist.

Tools, languages, and technologies used:

  • Data Science and Machine Learning: Python 3, Pandas, NumPy, and Scikit-Learn (PolynomialFeatures and LinearRegression) for predictive training and geospatial calculations.
  • Frontend and HUD Interface: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and the open-source mapping library Leaflet.js.
  • Backend, Storage, and Data: Supabase (cloud PostgreSQL database for the zonas_marte table and Storage for the panoramic basemap), along with structured data exchange in CSV and JSON.
  • Official Data from NASA and Partners: JPL Mars Trek, USGS Planetary Geologic Mapping Program (SIM 3292), Mars Perseverance Raw Images, Curiosity's Proposed Path, and NASA Worldview.
  • Development and Engineering Assistance: Strategic use of artificial intelligence (Claude and Gemini) to support web interface layout, module structuring, and scientific synthesis.

How is our project creative? We combine the rigor of predictive Machine Learning models with an immersive visual experience inspired by a space helmet HUD (Head-Up Display). We use a warm "Martian Horizon" color palette designed to prevent eye strain, animated beacons with radar waves, smooth camera fly-overs across the terrain, and integrated optical telemetry that simulates an astronaut's actual surface navigation dashboard.

Factors considered by the team: To ensure scientific accuracy and operational utility, our team (THE SUPERNOVA CODE) integrated five critical variables into the model and interface:

  1. Topography, elevation, and slopes (MOLA): Impact on the safe transit of rovers and astronauts.
  2. Surface thermal curves (THEMIS): Extreme day-and-night variations for spacesuit power management (PLSS).
  3. Radiation exposure (RAD): Critical thresholds (greater than 0.68 mSv/day) to define maximum excursion times.
  4. Spectral and mineralogical composition (CRISM/OMEGA/SHARAD): Identification of areas with bound water or buried ice.
  5. Surface visual validation: Integration of real photographs captured by the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers.
